1:
The occasion is placed in three different reigns. John Calvin holds it composed after David’s death, since although David had foreign kings among his enemies we do not read that they ever besieged Jerusalem and reduced it to an extremity requiring a wonderful manifestation of God’s power; he refers it rather to the time of king Ahaz. Keil and Delitzsch put it earlier: the mention of the kings points to an army of confederates, and the representation of the hostile powers by the shattered ships of Tarshish fits no period so well as the time of Jehoshaphat — though the coincidences with Isaiah, they add, do not prove the prophet its author. Adam Clarke puts it latest, referring it to the Jews returned from captivity and suggesting it was sung at the dedication of the second temple.

The title itself divides two voices sharply. Augustine of Hippo builds on the words for the second day of the week: on that day was made the firmament of heaven, and by the second day we ought to understand the Church of Christ — the Church in those written in heaven, who do not yield to this world’s temptations and are worthy of the name of firmament, the Apostle himself calling the Church the pillar and firmament of the truth. Adam Clarke records the same addition from the versions and dismisses it in a clause: for which, he says, he believes it would be difficult to find a meaning.

How the city can be the joy of the whole earth divides them again. Adam Clarke says commentators have been greatly puzzled by it, and cuts the knot by narrowing the noun: take the earth for the habitable globe and there is no sense in which Zion ever was its joy, but the Hebrew means the whole of this land and has no other meaning, the temple being the ornament and glory of Judea. John Wesley keeps the wider sense by making it prediction, the words being spoken prophetically because the gospel was to go from thence to all nations. Charles Ellicott works on the other half of the line: the word rendered situation is found only here and is explained from a cognate Arabic word to mean elevation, distinctive enough of Jerusalem, though an adverbial use, supremely beautiful, may be all the poet intends. The sides of the north is generally taken for the quarter of the north, but the words could equally mean secret recesses, giving a figure of the security to be found in God’s holy city — a thought taken up by the word refuge next verse. John Gill is content with the topography — an eminence in a wholesome air, Kidron gliding by, mountains all round — and reads the church into each feature.

The refuge is then read as shelter or as fortification. Adam Clarke offers both: all who worship in spirit and truth find God for their refuge, but the words may mean that God is known for the defence of her palaces, which agrees with the three verses following. Charles Ellicott presses the second, wanting prominence given to the idea of security from height — God among her castles is known as a high and secure tower. Keil and Delitzsch read the pointing as proof that the praise rests on a contemporary event, God having made himself known by the loftily built parts of the city as an inaccessible fortress. John Wesley thinks the palaces may be the king’s house and the temple, by protecting which God protected the city. Matthew Henry takes the title city of the great King as our Saviour did, to prove that swearing by Jerusalem is profanely swearing by God himself; and C.H. Spurgeon sets the acclamation against another, saying that instead of the mad cry of Ephesus, Great is Diana, we hear the self-evident testimony, Great is Jehovah.
4:
Which kings assembled is a question Charles Ellicott says cannot be answered. They were evidently known to the writer but are matter of merest conjecture to us: some suppose the kings of Ammon, Moab and Edom who attacked Jehoshaphat; others the tributary princes of Sennacherib, who in his annals, as lately deciphered, speaks of setting up viceroys in Phoenicia and Philistia; others, referring the psalm to the time of Ahaz, understand Pekah and Rezin. The touches of the picture, vivid as they are, are not so historically defined as to allow the question to be settled. John Wesley offers the first two of those candidates and no more, either the confederates against Jehoshaphat or the Assyrian princes whom their own people vaingloriously called kings. John Gill lists more instances still — the Philistine princes seeking David, the Ethiopians under Asa, the Moabites and Ammonites under Jehoshaphat, Syria and Israel under Ahaz, Sennacherib under Hezekiah — and then leaves them all behind, taking the verse of the latter day, when the kings of the earth, Pagan, Papal and Mahometan alike, will be gathered to the battle at Armageddon; Jarchi and Kimchi, he adds, understood it of Gog and Magog. Adam Clarke is interested less in their names than in their timing: neighbouring potentates had long envied the nation’s prosperity and coveted the riches of the temple, but had no power against it till the cup of transgression was full.

On the rout itself the roster is nearly unanimous and unusually vivid. C.H. Spurgeon makes the speed of it the point: they came and they went, no sooner together than scattered, coming one way and fleeing twenty; they came like foam on the angry sea, and like foam they melted away. He notices that the psalmist has put in a note of exclamation at the sight, and turns the verse on his own century, that even so shall the haters of the church vanish from the field, Papists, Ritualists, Arians and Sceptics each having their day and passing to the limbo of forgetfulness. Adam Clarke reaches the same end more drily: those who came to destroy were glad to make their own escape. On the looking, C.H. Spurgeon observes that they came and saw but did not conquer, there being no boast of coming, seeing and conquering for them, and Charles Ellicott notes independently that the verse has reminded commentators of the same Roman tag, adding that its force comes from the omission of the conjunctions, which the Authorised Version wrongly supplies: they looked, even so were terrified, bewildered, panic-struck.

What exactly they saw is read three ways. John Gill reports that Aben Ezra took it for the power of God and Jarchi for God himself going forth to fight against the nations, and applies it to the brightness of Christ’s spiritual reign and to the burning of Rome, whose smoke the kings of the earth will see and lament. John Wesley keeps it military: they did only look upon the city, and did not come into it, nor shoot an arrow there, nor cast a bank against it; what they marvelled at was the wonderful works wrought by God. Charles Ellicott will not say what they saw at all, only that they were panic-struck, and renders the next clause as sprung up in alarm.

The fear that seized them is located rather than described. John Gill puts it either at the moment they came up to the city, or, following Kimchi, in the very place where they had thought to make a great slaughter. John Wesley supplies a date instead, the tidings of an Egyptian king marching against them and the terrible slaughter of their army. C.H. Spurgeon is content with the image: where they hoped to triumph they quivered with dismay, held in the grip of Giant Despair; they did not take the city, but fear took hold of them.
7:
What Tarshish is gets three incompatible answers. John Gill rules out the usual candidates by name — not Tartessus in Spain, nor Tarsus in Cilicia, nor the port to which Jonah went and took shipping, but the sea in general — and offers the verse either as a simile for the dread that will seize the kings, which Kimchi and Aben Ezra compare to an east wind at sea breaking the ships, or as the manner in which the antichristian states will be destroyed, or as the loss of all the riches brought them in ships. Adam Clarke takes the very identification Gill refuses, conjecturing that ships of Tarshish were large stout vessels capable of making the voyage of Tarsus in Cilicia; and he passes on Calmet’s suggestion that the verse records the discomfiture of Cambyses, the same tempest striking dismay into his land forces and wrecking his fleet on the Mediterranean coast opposite his army, encamped in the valley of Jezreel. Charles Ellicott makes Tarshish a trade rather than a place: ships of Tarshish is a common term for large merchantmen, named from the traffic they plied, and here they are symbols of a powerful empire.

Whether any fleet was actually wrecked is a further question. Charles Ellicott grants it natural at first sight to connect the verse with the disaster to Jehoshaphat’s fleet, and allows that the event may have supplied the figure — but only a figure, and one for the dispersal of a land army, which he prefers to the suggestion that seaboard tribes were in the alliance and that the scattering of their armada ruined the enterprise. He supports the reading from Shakespeare, who in King John compares the rout of an army to a whole armada scattered and disjoined from fellowship by a roaring tempest on the flood. John Wesley reads it as a plain comparison of suddenness, God destroying these enemies no less violently than he sometimes destroys ships at sea with a fierce and vehement wind, such as the eastern winds were in those parts.

The next verse turns hearing into sight, and the roster differs over what had been heard. Matthew Henry takes it two ways at once: as we have heard done in former providences, so have we seen done in our own days, God’s latter appearances being consonant with his former; and as we have heard in the promise, so have we seen in the performance, since in the great things God does for his church it is good to notice the fulfilling of the scriptures, which helps us understand both the providence and the scripture fulfilled in it. Adam Clarke supplies the history his fathers had declared, the invasions by Assyrians, Syrians, Egyptians, Babylonians, Persians and the Greeks under Alexander. Charles Ellicott thinks it probably the ancient tale of the overthrow of Pharaoh and his host that recurred to the poet’s mind, the generations of a religious nation being bound each to each by natural piety. John Gill makes the words the people’s own observation on what precedes, and notes that Aben Ezra referred them to the war of Gog and Magog.

The closing promise is where they part. Charles Ellicott would render it that God will preserve her for ever, taking it as the refrain of the song and thinking it should probably be restored earlier in the psalm as well. Adam Clarke transfers it: this must refer to the true temple, the Christian Church, of which the Jewish Church was a type, for the type perished while the antitype remained and will remain till time shall be no more. John Wesley keeps the promise where it stands but attaches a condition to it, saying that God will defend her in all succeeding ages — and so he would have done, had Jerusalem not forsaken him and forfeited his protection.
9:
What the worshippers did in the temple turns on one verb. John Gill lays out the options: Jarchi read it as we have waited for thy lovingkindness, and some explain it of hope and expectation, the Syriac rendering it so and the word itself carrying the sense of tarrying; the Chaldee has we have esteemed thy goodness; while Menachem, Aben Ezra, Kimchi and Ben Melech render it as our version does, we have thought. He takes the last, noting that God has his set time to favour Zion and that till it comes his people do right to be hoping and waiting. C.H. Spurgeon settles on meditation and makes it a rule: holy men are thoughtful men, who do not suffer God’s wonders to pass before their eyes and melt into forgetfulness. It is well to think of past lovingkindness in times of trial and equally profitable in seasons of prosperity, since grateful memories sweeten sorrows and sober joys; and the place is fit for the thought, for where God is most seen he is best loved, the assembled saints themselves constituting a living temple. Hard by the table of shewbread that commemorates his bounty, he says, should stand the altar of incense that denotes our praise. Adam Clarke reads the same meditation as the hinge of the deliverance: we went to thy temple to worship, meditated on thy goodness and waited for a display of it, and the panic that first struck us was transferred to our enemies. John Wesley says only that it has been the matter of our serious and deep meditation when worshipping in thy temple. Charles Ellicott draws a conclusion about the psalm itself from the mention of the temple, saying the verse seems to indicate a liturgic origin for it.

The praise that answers the name is measured in three ways. Charles Ellicott takes name in the sense we give it in the phrase name and fame, so that God’s praise was up to the reputation his great deeds had won; and on the second clause he cannot resist the comparison — the right hand is not like Jove’s, as the heathen say, full of thunderbolts, but full of justice. Adam Clarke puts it as a proportion: as far as thou art known, so far art thou praised, and where thou art known thou wilt have praise to the end of the earth. John Wesley makes it a matter of testimony, that God is acknowledged to be such an one as he has affirmed himself to be in his Word. John Gill pushes it forward into the latter day, when the name will be great in all the earth and the Gospel, which is his name, will be preached to every nation and kindred and tongue. C.H. Spurgeon pushes it outward instead: the glory of these exploits overleaps the boundaries of earth, and what if men are silent, since the woods and seas and mountains with all their countless tribes are full of the divine praise — as in a shell we listen to the murmurs of the sea, so in the convolutions of creation we hear the praises of God.

The rejoicing is then addressed to a disputed party. Charles Ellicott denies that the daughters of Judah are the maidens of Jerusalem and takes them for the towns and villages of Judah, adding that the judgments named may carry the prominent idea of God’s customary dealings with his people rather than any single act. Adam Clarke keeps them human and gives them a reason: the temple, threatened with total destruction, is restored in majesty and repaired, and the daughters of Judah are glad that God has turned her captivity and poured out his judgments on her oppressors. John Wesley glosses those judgments simply as falling on thine and their enemies, and John Gill takes Mount Zion here for the church in general.
12:
Who is told to walk about Zion is not obvious. John Gill canvasses three possibilities: the words may be an address to the enemies of the church, sarcastically delivered, calling them to besiege her and see what the issue will be; or, as Jarchi took it, to the builders, to survey what repairs were necessary; or rather to the saints themselves, to view the strength of the church for their own encouragement and to report it to others. C.H. Spurgeon has no doubt it is the church’s own people, and makes the circuit a discipline: beat her bounds often, as Israel marched around Jericho, encircling her with loving perambulations, since we cannot too deeply consider the origin, privileges, history and security of the church. Her foes counted her towers first in envy and then in terror; we should count them with sacred exultation. He gives the figure a modern setting too, recalling the walled city of Lucerne with its succession of towers, and how in going round it and pausing at each he had realised the lingering inspection the metaphor implies. Adam Clarke keeps to the survey, bidding the reader consider the magnificence of the temple and count the towers by which it is fortified. John Wesley supplies the result: they are to mark her towers and palaces with thankfulness, since upon enquiry they will find not one of them demolished. Charles Ellicott glosses the verb, noting that tell here means count, as it does in Milton’s shepherd who tells his tale, that is, counts his sheep.

What the bulwarks are is read literally and figuratively. Adam Clarke means real redoubts, and adds a purpose to the register: make an exact account of the whole, that you may have something to tell your children of how Jerusalem was built in troublesome times and how God put it into the hearts of the heathen to assist in adorning the temple. Charles Ellicott works on the verb again: the word rendered consider is peculiar to this passage and its root idea seems to be divide, so that to divide her palaces means to take them one by one and regard them. John Gill makes every rampart a doctrine — the free favour of God in Christ, his everlasting love, the covenant with its blessings, the power of God surrounding the church as the mountains did Jerusalem, and the righteousness of Christ appointed for walls and bulwarks — and notes that some render the clause set your hearts on her strength. C.H. Spurgeon uses the verse to defend a doctrine against those who abuse it: the security of the people of God is not to be kept in the background but may be safely taught and frequently pondered, and only to base hearts will it prove harmful, since the sons of perdition make a stumbling stone even of the Lord Jesus himself. We are not to turn away from inspecting Zion’s ramparts, he says, because idlers skulk behind them.

The last words of the psalm are disputed out of existence by one voice. Charles Ellicott holds that the phrase rendered unto death is proved by the ancient versions and by variant readings to be really a musical direction, either placed at the end instead of the beginning or shifted back from the title of the psalm that follows. Adam Clarke keeps it and leans on it: God will guide us through all the snares of life and will never leave us, and even unto and in death he will be our portion, being just such a God as we need, infinite in mercy, goodness and truth. John Gill reads the opening demonstrative as pointing to God as if visible, which he takes of Christ manifest in the flesh, distinguishing him from the gods of the Gentiles and claiming him as the covenant God whose relation to his people will always continue.
